Limitations: (1) Precision only, no recall. (2) Doesn't capture meaning/semantics. (3) Requires multiple references for best results. (4) Doesn't handle synonyms well. (5) May reward short, safe translations. Alternatives: METEOR (synonyms, stemming), TER (edit distance), BERTScore (semantic similarity via embeddings). Used in: machine translation, text summarization, text generation evaluation.
explanation: BLEU is the standard automatic metric for text generation, but understanding its limitations is crucial.
betterAnswer: BLEU: n-gram precision + brevity penalty. Score 0-100. Measures surface overlap, not semantics. Limitations: precision-only, no synonyms, needs multiple references. Alternatives: METEOR, BERTScore. Good >0.6, acceptable >0.4.

question: What is an LLM?
expectedAnswer: LLM (Large Language Model): a neural network with billions of parameters, trained on massive text corpora, capable of generating and understanding natural language. Architecture: typically decoder-only Transformer (GPT series). Key characteristics: (1) Scale: billions of parameters (GPT-3: 175B, GPT-4: estimated 1.8T). (2) Training: unsupervised pretraining (next token prediction) on internet text. (3) Capabilities: text generation, translation, summarization, QA, reasoning, code generation. (4) Emergent abilities: few-shot learning, chain-of-thought reasoning (appear at scale). (5) Inference: autoregressive generation (predict one token at a time). Training pipeline: pretraining → instruction tuning → RLHF/DPO → deployment. Applications: chatbots, content creation, coding assistants, research, education. Limitations: hallucination, bias, high compute cost, knowledge cutoff, reasoning limitations.
explanation: LLMs are the most impactful AI technology of the 2020s. Understanding their capabilities and limitations is essential.
betterAnswer: LLM: billions-parameter Transformer trained on massive text. Decoder-only (GPT). Capabilities: generation, translation, QA, reasoning, code. Emergent: few-shot, chain-of-thought. Training: pretrain → instruction tune → RLHF. Limitations: hallucination, bias, compute cost.

question: How does a Transformer-based LLM work?
expectedAnswer: Transformer-based LLM works: (1) Tokenization: text → tokens (BPE). (2) Embedding: tokens → vectors + positional encoding. (3) Decoder stack: multiple layers of masked self-attention + feed-forward. Masked attention prevents attending to future tokens. (4) Output: probability distribution over vocabulary for next token. (5) Generation: sample from distribution (temperature, top-k, top-p), append to sequence, repeat. Training: (1) Pretraining: predict next token on trillions of tokens (massive compute). (2) Instruction tuning: fine-tune on instruction-response pairs. (3) RLHF: align with human preferences via reward model + PPO. Key innovations: (1) Self-attention: captures long-range dependencies. (2) Parallel processing: efficient training. (3) Scaling laws: performance improves predictably with scale. (4) In-context learning: few-shot examples in prompt. (5) Chain-of-thought: step-by-step reasoning. Emergent capabilities at scale: arithmetic, code generation, logical reasoning.
explanation: Understanding how LLMs work from architecture to training explains their remarkable capabilities and limitations.
betterAnswer: LLM: tokenize → embed + positional → decoder stack (masked self-attention + FFN) → next token probability → autoregressive generation. Training: pretrain (next token) → instruction tune → RLHF. Self-attention + scaling = emergent capabilities.

question: What is an embedding?
expectedAnswer: Embedding: a learned mapping from discrete symbols (words, tokens, entities) to dense continuous vectors in a lower-dimensional space. Purpose: (1) Capture semantic meaning (similar items → similar vectors). (2) Enable mathematical operations on discrete data. (3) Provide input for ML models. Types: (1) Word embeddings: Word2Vec, GloVe, FastText — static (same vector regardless of context). (2) Contextual embeddings: BERT, GPT — dynamic (same word different vectors in different contexts). (3) Sentence/document embeddings: encode entire texts. (4) Entity/item embeddings: for non-text entities (users, products). Properties: (1) Dense (typically 100-768 dimensions). (2) Semantic similarity via cosine similarity. (3) Analogical relationships (king - man + woman ≈ queen). (4) Learned from data (not hand-crafted). In LLMs: token embeddings are the first layer, projecting token IDs to dense vectors before transformer processing. Foundation for: search (semantic search), recommendations, classification, clustering.
explanation: Embeddings are the bridge between discrete data and continuous vector space, fundamental to modern ML.
betterAnswer: Embedding: mapping discrete symbols → dense vectors. Captures semantics (similar → similar vectors). Types: word (Word2Vec, static), contextual (BERT, dynamic), sentence, entity. Properties: dense, semantic similarity, analogies. In LLMs: first layer of transformer.

question: What is a vector database?
expectedAnswer: Vector database: specialized database optimized for storing, indexing, and querying high-dimensional vectors (embeddings). Purpose: enable fast similarity search (find vectors most similar to a query vector). Key operations: (1) Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) search: find top-k similar vectors efficiently. (2) Indexing: algorithms for fast retrieval (HNSW, IVF, LSH). (3) CRUD operations with vector support. Why needed: (1) Exact search in high dimensions is O(n) — too slow for millions/billions of vectors. (2) ANN provides sub-linear time search. (3) Specialized indexing (HNSW graph, inverted files) enables real-time search. Popular databases: (1) Pinecone: managed, cloud-native. (2) Weaviate: open-source, GraphQL API. (3) Milvus: open-source, scalable. (4) FAISS: library (not database), Facebook's similarity search. (5) Chroma: lightweight, developer-friendly. (6) pgvector: PostgreSQL extension. Applications: RAG (retrieve context), semantic search, recommendation systems, image search, deduplication. Key metrics: recall@k, QPS, latency.
explanation: Vector databases are essential infrastructure for modern AI applications, especially RAG systems.
betterAnswer: Vector DB: stores/indexes high-dimensional vectors, enables fast similarity search (ANN). Algorithms: HNSW, IVF, LSH. Options: Pinecone, Weaviate, Milvus, FAISS (library), Chroma, pgvector. Applications: RAG, semantic search, recommendations, image search.

question: What is RAG?
expectedAnswer: RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) combines information retrieval with text generation. Pipeline: (1) Indexing: chunk documents → embed with embedding model → store in vector database. (2) Retrieval: embed query → find top-k relevant chunks via similarity search. (3) Augmentation: concatenate retrieved chunks with original query as context. (4) Generation: LLM generates answer using context + query. Benefits: (1) Reduces hallucination (grounds in factual documents). (2) Enables knowledge updates without retraining. (3) Provides source citations. (4) Reduces LLM's knowledge cutoff problem. Challenges: (1) Chunk size optimization (too small: loses context, too large: noise). (2) Retrieval quality (wrong context → wrong answers). (3) Context window limits (can't fit all retrieved docs). (4) Relevance filtering (exclude irrelevant retrieved chunks). Advanced: hybrid search (dense + sparse), re-ranking, query transformation, multi-hop retrieval, self-RAG. Evaluation: retrieval recall, answer faithfulness, relevance.
explanation: RAG is the primary approach for building factual, grounded LLM applications.
betterAnswer: RAG: index (chunk → embed → vector DB) → retrieve (query embed → top-k similarity) → augment (context + query) → generate (LLM). Benefits: reduces hallucination, updatable knowledge, citations. Challenges: chunk size, retrieval quality, context limits. Advanced: hybrid search, re-ranking.

question: Why use RAG instead of fine-tuning?
expectedAnswer: RAG vs Fine-tuning comparison: RAG: retrieves relevant documents at inference time, provides them as context to LLM. Model unchanged. Fine-tuning: continues training LLM on domain-specific data, modifying model weights. Key differences: (1) Knowledge update: RAG updates instantly (change documents), fine-tuning requires retraining. (2) Cost: RAG cheaper (no retraining), fine-tuning expensive (GPU hours). (3) Accuracy: fine-tuning can be more accurate for domain-specific tasks, RAG better for factual recall. (4) Hallucination: RAG reduces by grounding in documents, fine-tuning may hallucinate on unseen topics. (5) Infrastructure: RAG needs vector DB + retrieval pipeline, fine-tuning needs training infrastructure. When to use RAG: (1) Knowledge changes frequently. (2) Need citations/sources. (3) Large, evolving knowledge base. (4) Budget constraints. When to fine-tune: (1) Domain-specific style/format. (2) Consistent behavior needed. (3) No external knowledge retrieval needed. (4) Privacy concerns (can't send data to external API). Hybrid: RAG + fine-tuning for best of both.
explanation: Understanding when to use RAG vs fine-tuning is critical for building effective LLM applications.
betterAnswer: RAG: retrieve at inference, model unchanged, updatable, cheaper, grounds in documents. Fine-tuning: modify weights, domain-specific, more accurate for style, expensive. RAG for changing knowledge + citations. Fine-tuning for consistent behavior + privacy. Hybrid possible.
